claims.text: As-received, pre-exposure Q235 steel has an intact native oxide film.
The integrity of the native oxide film governs the onset and progression of corrosion-related degradation in Q235 steel.
Selective removal of the native oxide film will accelerate localized corrosion of Q235 steel in chloride-rich environments.
Controlled reoxidation that restores a passivation layer will suppress corrosion relative to oxide-stripped Q235 steel.
A mild chemical etch can selectively remove the native oxide without altering the underlying Q235 microstructure.
The native oxide or passivation film acts as a barrier to aggressive ions.
An intact native oxide film limits chloride ingress into untreated Q235 steel.
Limiting chloride ingress through an oxide film retards localized pitting corrosion.
Removing the native oxide exposes the underlying Q235 metal.
Exposure of the underlying metal facilitates chloride adsorption and defect initiation.
Chloride adsorption and defect initiation accelerate corrosion.
Re-forming a controlled oxide film restores barrier properties and mitigates corrosion.
Oxide-stripped Q235 samples will have lower pitting potentials than untreated samples.
Oxide-stripped Q235 samples will have higher corrosion current densities than untreated samples.
Oxide-stripped Q235 samples will exhibit more pronounced localized attack than untreated samples.
Reoxidized Q235 samples will exhibit corrosion behavior comparable to, or only slightly different from, the untreated baseline.
Exposure at approximately 60–80°C provides accelerated chloride-corrosion conditions relative to room temperature.
The proposed mechanism is applicable only if surface treatments leave the bulk microstructure unchanged and corrosion is dominated by chloride-induced localized attack.
